cells.tense: You are tending something right now, and you know its real pace.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and name out loud what it actually needs this week — then let the outcome be what it is.
cells.core:
You're feeding something that isn't finished yet. That's the whole work, and you do it with an attention most people save for emergencies — you notice what a person or a project needs before the need gets loud, and you supply it in the amount it needs. The care isn't performed. It's practical, and it reaches people.

What keeps this clean is that you know when your part is done. The thing you're growing doesn't need more of you once it's grown; it needs you to step back and let what you raised stand on its own. That release isn't walking away. It's the end of a job you finished, and it leaves both of you in better contact than the work did.
cells.sheetLine: You grow things by attention, and you know when to let go.
cells.verb: tending what grows, learning its shape by hand
cells.place: in the room where two people are trying to stay in contact

cells.tense: You'll have arranged every next step before the present one has had a chance to land.
cells.ask: For one thing you're growing, hand it to the person involved and say what you hope happens — then do nothing about it today.
cells.core:
You're managing people forward. Where something is still taking shape, you've already got the version of it that should exist, and you're quietly steering the people involved toward it — tidied, timed, accounted for. The caring is real. But it's arriving ahead of the thing itself, and the person on the other end can feel the schedule under the warmth.

Care that clutches doesn't get a return. Let the situation look like what it actually looks like right now, unfinished and yours to help with only as much as it needs. That's how you hold space instead of managing it. Aim a little wonder at what hasn't arrived yet. The thing doesn't have to be finished before it is allowed to be here.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that closed, with your hands still full.
cells.ask: Tend one small growing thing this week with no one watching — a plant, a habit, a piece of work — and let it be enough on its own.
cells.core:
Nothing's growing through your hands right now. You can see it — people around you feel distant, or gone, or hard to reach — and what's been happening is you report the distance instead of entering it. You still want to help. It's just stopped moving toward anything.

Don't wait to feel like a helper before you help. Pick something small that's alive or unfinished and give it a little of your attention every few days, with nobody around to see it work. Something is allowed to grow because you showed up for it. Your own push, aimed at that, comes back around to the people part on its own. Starting quietly is fine.
cells.sheetLine: You want to help, and you've stopped moving toward it.

cells.tense: You are tending and shaping what's around you here, and describing none of it as your own.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been building in a relationship and say plainly that it matters to you, then wait for what comes back.
cells.core:
You keep things connected around here without counting it as anything. You notice what matters to the people in the room, you adjust, you hold what needs holding, you make the small repairs nobody asks for — and you'd call all of it just getting along. The work is real. Calling it yours isn't.

There's a finish to this kind of care that you keep skipping: acknowledging it, in front of someone, once. When you've finished tending something, say so, and whose it is, before you decide what it meant. That's the release — not giving up, but the last act of a job you did yourself. Being straight about it is not a boast. It lets the person you helped answer you instead of just receiving.

attempts.check: The record says the person learns how living things grow by tending them; I could be wrong that they are tending anything at all, or that tending, not distance, is what showed up in their connections. If I'm wrong, the ask still costs them nothing but a minute and an observation, and it needs no one else present to work. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you are already growing this' — it stays out; they know what they have or haven't been doing, and I don't.
